questions.q: In a classic experiment, one group was randomly given a coffee mug and asked the minimum price they'd accept to sell it; a separate group, given no mug, was asked the maximum price they'd pay for an identical one. Ownership was assigned purely by coin flip. What did researchers consistently find?
choices: Sellers and buyers named almost identical prices, since the mug's value didn't depend on who happened to hold it
Both groups refused to name any price, since assigning a dollar value to a gift feels unethical
Sellers demanded roughly twice as much as buyers were willing to pay, purely because of random ownership — the endowment effect
Buyers were willing to pay roughly twice as much as sellers demanded, since new owners undervalue unfamiliar items

questions.q: What is the name of the philosophical paradox in which a hypothetical donkey, placed exactly midway between two identical, equally appealing piles of hay, is unable to find any rational reason to choose one over the other — and, in the paradox, starves to death from indecision?

A disease is expected to kill 600 people. Framed as 'lives saved,' Program A saves 200 people for certain and Program B has a 1-in-3 chance of saving all 600 (and 2-in-3 chance of saving no one) — most people pick the certain option, Program A. The identical choice is then reframed as 'lives lost': Program C causes 400 deaths for certain, and Program D has a 1-in-3 chance nobody dies (and 2-in-3 chance all 600 die). Even though Program A = Program C and Program B = Program D in every outcome, most people now switch and pick Program D. What is this reversal called?

Weigh it — a hard-boiled egg is heavier
